questions.a: Probability is a numerical measure, lying between 0 and 1, of how likely an event is to occur. For a finite sample space S with equally likely outcomes, the classical definition is P(E) = n(E)/n(S), the number of outcomes favourable to E divided by the total number of outcomes. Axiomatically, P is a set function satisfying 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1 for every event, P(S) = 1, and P(E₁ ∪ E₂) = P(E₁) + P(E₂) whenever E₁ and E₂ are mutually exclusive. P(E) = 0 means E is impossible, while P(E) = 1 means E is certain. The ratio formula is valid only when all outcomes are equally likely, whereas the axioms hold for every probability model.
steps: Identify the sample space S of all possible outcomes of the experiment
Count the favourable outcomes n(E) and the total outcomes n(S)
For equally likely outcomes apply P(E) = n(E)/n(S)
Verify the axioms: 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1, P(S) = 1, additivity for disjoint events
questions.formula: Classical: P(E) = n(E)/n(S), with 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1 and P(S) = 1
questions.explanation: This is the classical and axiomatic definition that underlies every probability calculation; the simple ratio formula is valid only when outcomes are equally likely.
questions.oneShotPreview: Probability = favourable outcomes / total equally likely outcomes; a number in [0,1].

questions.q: 1 b) Evaluate P(A/B), if P(A) = 7/13, P(B) = 9/13 and P(A ∩ B) = 4/13. [L5][CO2] [2M]
questions.a: The conditional probability of A given B is defined as P(A/B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B), provided P(B) > 0; here P(B) = 9/13 ≠ 0. Substituting the joint probability gives P(A/B) = (4/13)/(9/13). Since the common denominator 13 cancels, this becomes (4/13) × (13/9) = 4/9. The given value P(A) = 7/13 is not needed for this calculation; it would only be used to test consistency or to find the reverse probability P(B/A). Hence P(A/B) = 4/9.
steps: Write the conditional formula P(A/B) = P(A∩B)/P(B)
Cancel the common factor 13 to obtain 4/9
questions.explanation: Conditioning on B restricts the sample space to B, so the chance of A inside it is the joint probability divided by P(B).

questions.a: Bayes' theorem converts a known forward conditional probability into the required reverse conditional probability. Let B₁, B₂, ..., Bₙ form a partition of the sample space S (mutually exclusive and exhaustive) with P(Bᵢ) > 0, and let A be any event with P(A) > 0. Then P(Bᵢ/A) = P(Bᵢ)P(A/Bᵢ) / Σⱼ P(Bⱼ)P(A/Bⱼ). The denominator is precisely P(A) by the law of total probability. In words, posterior probability = (prior probability × likelihood) / evidence, where each Bᵢ is a hypothesis and P(Bᵢ/A) is its updated probability after observing A.
steps: Assume B₁, ..., Bₙ partition S with every P(Bᵢ) > 0 and P(A) > 0
Express the joint probability two ways: P(Bᵢ∩A) = P(Bᵢ)P(A/Bᵢ) = P(A)P(Bᵢ/A)
Solve for the reverse probability: P(Bᵢ/A) = P(Bᵢ)P(A/Bᵢ)/P(A)
Replace P(A) with Σⱼ P(Bⱼ)P(A/Bⱼ) from the law of total probability
questions.explanation: Bayes' theorem converts a known conditional probability P(A/Bi) into the unknown reverse probability P(Bi/A) using the partition and the law of total probability.
questions.oneShotPreview: P(Bi|A) = P(Bi)P(A|Bi) / Σ P(Bj)P(A|Bj) — prior × likelihood / evidence.

questions.q: 1 d) Explain types of random variables. [L2][CO2] [2M]
questions.a: A random variable X is a real-valued function on the sample space, and its type determines how probabilities are computed. A discrete random variable takes a finite or countably infinite set of values (for example, the number of heads in three tosses) and is described by a probability mass function p(x) = P(X = x) with Σ p(x) = 1. A continuous random variable takes any value in an interval (for example, height or time) and is described by a probability density function f(x) ≥ 0 with ∫f(x)dx = 1, where P(a < X < b) = ∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx. Mixed variables possess both a discrete and a continuous component. Binomial and Poisson are discrete; uniform, exponential and normal are continuous.
steps: Classify X according to the nature of its set of possible values
Discrete case: countable values, use a PMF p(x) with Σp(x) = 1
Continuous case: interval of values, use a PDF f(x) with ∫f(x)dx = 1
Note that mixed variables combine both cases, then cite examples of each type
questions.formula: Discrete: p(x)=P(X=x), Σp(x)=1; Continuous: P(a<X<b)=∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx
questions.explanation: The distinction decides whether probabilities are found by summing a PMF (discrete) or integrating a PDF (continuous).
questions.oneShotPreview: Discrete = countable values with a PMF; continuous = interval values with a PDF.

questions.q: 1 e) Define expected value of a discrete random variable. [L1][CO2] [2M]
questions.a: The expected value (mean) of a discrete random variable X with probability mass function p(x) is E(X) = Σ x·p(x), summed over all possible values of X. It is the probability-weighted average of those values, and more generally E[g(X)] = Σ g(x)·p(x). The expectation is the long-run average value observed when the experiment is repeated a very large number of times, even though it need not itself be a possible value of X. When the distribution is symmetric, the mean equals the centre of symmetry.
steps: List all possible values x of the discrete variable X
Write the PMF p(x) = P(X=x) for each value
Multiply each value by its probability and sum: E(X) = Σ x·p(x)
Interpret the result as the long-run average over repeated trials
questions.formula: E(X) = Σ x·p(x)   (more generally E[g(X)] = Σ g(x)·p(x))
questions.explanation: Weighting each possible value by its probability gives the centre of the distribution, the quantity that remains stable across repeated trials.
questions.oneShotPreview: E(X) = Σ x·p(x); the probability-weighted long-run average.

questions.q: 2 a) A class consists of 6 girls and 10 boys. If a committee of 3 is chosen at random from the class, find the Probability that (i) 3 boys are selected (ii) Exactly 2 girls are selected. [L1][CO2] [5M]
questions.a: There are 6 + 10 = 16 students, and since every committee of 3 is equally likely we count combinations. The total number of committees is C(16,3) = (16·15·14)/(3·2·1) = 560. (i) Choosing all 3 members from the 10 boys gives C(10,3) = (10·9·8)/(3·2·1) = 120, so P = 120/560 = 3/14. (ii) Exactly 2 girls means 2 of the 6 girls and 1 of the 10 boys, so the favourable count is C(6,2)·C(10,1) = 15·10 = 150 and P = 150/560 = 15/56.
questions.formula: Classical: P(E) = favourable combinations / C(16,3) = favourable / 560
questions.explanation: Every committee of 3 is equally likely, so each probability is the number of favourable combinations divided by the total number of combinations.

questions.q: 2 b) If three coins are tossed. Find the probability of getting i) 3 heads ii) 2 heads only iii) no heads. [L1][CO2] [5M]
questions.a: Three fair coins give 2³ = 8 equally likely ordered outcomes, so each outcome has probability 1/8. (i) Three heads occurs only for HHH, so P = 1/8. (ii) Exactly two heads occurs for HHT, HTH and THH, i.e. C(3,2) = 3 outcomes, so P = 3/8. (iii) No heads occurs only for TTT, so P = 1/8. Equivalently, the number of heads is Binomial(n = 3, p = 1/2) with P(X = k) = C(3,k)/8.
steps: (ii) 2 heads: C(3,2) = 3 outcomes (HHT, HTH, THH), P = 3/8
questions.explanation: This uses the classical definition: count the outcomes matching each event and divide by the 8 equally likely outcomes.

questions.q: 3 a) Two cards are selected at random from 10 cards numbered 1 to 10. Find the probability that the sum is even if (i) The two cards are drawn together. (ii) The two cards drawn one after other with replacement. [L5][CO2] [5M]
questions.a: Among the cards numbered 1 to 10 there are 5 odd and 5 even numbers, and the sum is even exactly when both cards have the same parity (odd + odd or even + even). (i) Drawn together (without replacement), the total pairs are C(10,2) = 45 and the favourable pairs are C(5,2) + C(5,2) = 10 + 10 = 20, so P = 20/45 = 4/9. (ii) With replacement the draws are independent and P(odd) = P(even) = 5/10 = 1/2 on each draw, so P(even sum) = (1/2)(1/2) + (1/2)(1/2) = 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2.
steps: Classify the cards: 5 odd, 5 even; an even sum needs both odd or both even
(i) Without replacement: total = C(10,2) = 45; favourable = C(5,2)+C(5,2) = 20; P = 20/45 = 4/9
(ii) With replacement: P(odd) = P(even) = 5/10 = 1/2 on each draw
questions.formula: Without replacement: P = [C(5,2)+C(5,2)]/C(10,2); with replacement: P = p² + p²
questions.explanation: Odd+odd and even+even are the only ways to obtain an even sum; with replacement the chance of each draw being odd or even stays at 1/2.
questions.oneShotPreview: Even sum: 4/9 without replacement, 1/2 with replacement.

questions.q: 3 b) Determine (i) P(B/A) (ii) P(A/B^c) if A and B are events with P(A) = 1/3, P(B) = 1/4, P(A ∪ B) = 1/2. [L5][CO2] [5M]
questions.a: The addition rule P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B) supplies the missing joint probability. Rearranging, P(A ∩ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∪ B) = 1/3 + 1/4 − 1/2 = 4/12 + 3/12 − 6/12 = 1/12. (i) P(B/A) = P(A ∩ B)/P(A) = (1/12)/(1/3) = 1/4. (ii) The part of A outside B has probability P(A ∩ Bᶜ) = P(A) − P(A ∩ B) = 1/3 − 1/12 = 1/4, while P(Bᶜ) = 1 − 1/4 = 3/4, so P(A/Bᶜ) = (1/4)/(3/4) = 1/3.
steps: From the addition rule, P(A∩B) = P(A)+P(B)−P(A∪B)
questions.explanation: The addition rule supplies the missing joint probability, and each conditional probability is the appropriate joint probability divided by the probability of the given event.

questions.q: 4 a) In a certain town 40% have brown hair, 25% have brown eyes and 15% have both brown hair and brown eyes. A person is selected at random from the town. i) If he has brown hair, what is the probability that he has brown eyes also? ii) If he has brown eyes, determine the probability that he does not have brown hair? [L1][CO2] [5M]
questions.a: Let H denote brown hair and E denote brown eyes, so P(H) = 0.40, P(E) = 0.25 and P(H ∩ E) = 0.15. (i) Conditioning on brown hair restricts the sample space to H, so P(E/H) = P(H ∩ E)/P(H) = 0.15/0.40 = 3/8 = 0.375. (ii) The people with brown eyes but not brown hair have probability P(Hᶜ ∩ E) = P(E) − P(H ∩ E) = 0.25 − 0.15 = 0.10. Since we condition on E, P(Hᶜ/E) = 0.10/0.25 = 2/5 = 0.4.
steps: Define H = brown hair, E = brown eyes: P(H)=0.40, P(E)=0.25, P(H∩E)=0.15
questions.explanation: A conditional probability restricts the sample space to the given characteristic, so only the part of the joint event lying inside that characteristic is counted.

questions.q: 4 b) The probability that students A,B,C,D solve the problem are 1/3, 2/5, 1/5 and 1/4 respectively If all of them try to solve the problem, What is the probability that the problem is solved? [L3][CO2] [5M]
questions.a: Assume the four students work independently. The problem is solved if at least one of them succeeds, so it is easier to use the complement: the problem stays unsolved only when all four fail. Their failure probabilities are 1 − 1/3 = 2/3, 1 − 2/5 = 3/5, 1 − 1/5 = 4/5 and 1 − 1/4 = 3/4. By independence these multiply, giving P(none solves) = (2/3)(3/5)(4/5)(3/4) = (2/5)(3/5) = 6/25 = 0.24. Therefore P(problem is solved) = 1 − 6/25 = 19/25 = 0.76.
steps: P(A)=1/3, P(B)=2/5, P(C)=1/5, P(D)=1/4; assume independence
questions.formula: Complement + independence: P(at least one solves) = 1 − Π(1 − pᵢ)
questions.explanation: It is easier to use the complement: the problem stays unsolved only when all four fail, and independence lets their failure probabilities multiply.

questions.q: 5 Two dice are thrown. Let A be the event that the sum of the point on the faces is 9. Let B be the event that at least one number is 6. Find (i) P(A ∩ B) (ii) P(A ∪ B) (iii) P(A^c ∪ B^c) (iv) P(A^c ∩ B^c) (v) P(A ∩ B^c) [L1][CO2] [10M]
questions.a: Two dice give 36 equally likely ordered pairs. A (sum 9) = {(3,6),(4,5),(5,4),(6,3)}, so P(A) = 4/36; B (at least one 6) has 11 outcomes, so P(B) = 11/36; and A ∩ B = {(3,6),(6,3)}, so P(A ∩ B) = 2/36 = 1/18. (i) P(A ∩ B) = 1/18. (ii) By the addition rule, P(A ∪ B) = 4/36 + 11/36 − 2/36 = 13/36. (iii) By De Morgan's law, P(Aᶜ ∪ Bᶜ) = 1 − P(A ∩ B) = 1 − 2/36 = 17/18. (iv) P(Aᶜ ∩ Bᶜ) = 1 − P(A ∪ B) = 1 − 13/36 = 23/36. (v) P(A ∩ Bᶜ) = P(A) − P(A ∩ B) = 4/36 − 2/36 = 2/36 = 1/18.
questions.explanation: Counting the outcomes in A, B and A ∩ B and then applying the addition rule, complement rule and De Morgan's laws yields all five requested probabilities.

questions.q: 6 In a certain college 25% of boys and 10% of girls are studying mathematics. The girls Constitute 60% of the student body. (a) What is the probability that mathematics is being studied? (b) If a student is selected at random and is found to be studying mathematics, find the probability that the student is a girl? (c) a boy [L1][CO2] [10M]
questions.a: Let G be girl, B be boy and M be studying mathematics, with P(G) = 0.6, P(B) = 0.4, P(M/G) = 0.10 and P(M/B) = 0.25. (a) By the law of total probability, P(M) = P(G)P(M/G) + P(B)P(M/B) = 0.6(0.10) + 0.4(0.25) = 0.06 + 0.10 = 0.16. (b) By Bayes' theorem, P(G/M) = P(G)P(M/G)/P(M) = 0.06/0.16 = 3/8 = 0.375. (c) Similarly P(B/M) = P(B)P(M/B)/P(M) = 0.10/0.16 = 5/8 = 0.625, which also equals 1 − 3/8.
steps: Priors P(G)=0.6, P(B)=0.4; likelihoods P(M|G)=0.10, P(M|B)=0.25
questions.explanation: Total probability gives the overall rate of studying mathematics, and Bayes' theorem reverses it to identify which group a randomly selected mathematics student belongs to.

questions.q: 7 Two dice are thrown. Let X assign to each point (a, b) in S the maximum of its numbers i.e, X(a,b)= max (a,b). Find the probability distribution. X is a random variable with X(s)={1,2,3,4,5,6}. Also find the mean and variance of the distribution. [L5][CO2] [10M]
steps: For X = k, count the 2k−1 ordered pairs whose maximum is k
questions.explanation: Counting the 2k-1 pairs whose maximum is k builds the PMF, and the formulas E(X)=sum x p(x) and Var(X)=E(X^2)-[E(X)]^2 give the mean and variance.

questions.q: 8 A random variable X has the following probability function: X = 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7 with P(x) = 0, K, 2K, 2K, 3K, K^2, 2K^2, 7K^2+K. Determine (i) K (ii) Evaluate P(X>=6) and P(0<X<5) (iii) if P(X<=K)>1/2, find the minimum value of K (iv) variance. [L5][CO2] [10M]
questions.a: The probabilities must sum to 1, so 0 + K + 2K + 2K + 3K + K² + 2K² + (7K² + K) = 9K + 10K² = 1. (i) Solving 10K² + 9K − 1 = 0 gives K = (−9 ± 11)/20, and the admissible positive root is K = 1/10. (ii) With K = 0.1 the probabilities are 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.2, 0.3, 0.01, 0.02, 0.17, so P(X ≥ 6) = 2K² + (7K² + K) = 9K² + K = 0.19 and P(0 < X < 5) = K + 2K + 2K + 3K = 8K = 0.8. (iii) Reading K here as the value k of X, the cumulative probabilities are P(X ≤ 3) = 0.5 and P(X ≤ 4) = 0.8, so the minimum k with P(X ≤ k) > 1/2 is 4. (iv) E(X) = 3.66 and E(X²) = 16.8, hence Var(X) = 16.8 − (3.66)² = 3.4044.
questions.explanation: Normalising the PMF fixes K; every other quantity is then found by summing the appropriate probabilities and applying Var(X)=E(X^2)-[E(X)]^2.

questions.q: 9 a) Find the mean and variance of the uniform probability distribution given by f(x) = 1/n for x = 1,2,...,n. [L1][CO2] [5M]
questions.a: For the discrete uniform distribution on x = 1, 2, ..., n, each outcome has probability 1/n. The mean is E(X) = (1/n)Σx = (1/n)·n(n+1)/2 = (n+1)/2. The second moment is E(X²) = (1/n)Σx² = (1/n)·n(n+1)(2n+1)/6 = (n+1)(2n+1)/6. Therefore Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]² = (n+1)(2n+1)/6 − (n+1)²/4 = (n²−1)/12 after putting both terms over the common denominator 12.
questions.explanation: Substituting the standard sums of the first n integers and their squares into the moment formulas gives closed-form mean and variance.

questions.q: a) If a random variable has a Probability density f(x) as f(x) = {2e^{-2x}, for x > 0; 0, for x <= 0}. Find the Probabilities that it will take on a value (i) Between 1&3 (ii) Greater than 0.5 [L1][CO2] [5M]
questions.a: This is the exponential distribution with rate 2, and ∫₀^∞ 2e^{−2x}dx = 1 confirms it is a valid density. (i) P(1 < X < 3) = ∫₁³ 2e^{−2x}dx = [−e^{−2x}]₁³ = e^{−2} − e^{−6} ≈ 0.1353 − 0.0025 = 0.1329. (ii) P(X > 0.5) = ∫₀.₅^∞ 2e^{−2x}dx = [−e^{−2x}]₀.₅^∞ = e^{−1} ≈ 0.3679. In general, for this density P(X > a) = e^{−2a}, so the tail probability at a = 0.5 is e^{−1} ≈ 0.3679.
steps: Identify f(x) = 2e^{−2x}, x > 0 as exponential with rate 2
questions.explanation: Integrating the density over the required interval gives the probability, and for an exponential density the tail integral from a to infinity simplifies to e^{-2a}.

questions.q: 10 A continuous random variable has the probability density function. f(x) = {k(1 - x^2); 0 < x < 1; 0; Otherwise}. Determine i) Constant 'k' ii) Mean and iii) Variance. [L5][CO2] [10M]
questions.a: The density is f(x) = k(1 − x²) for 0 < x < 1 and zero otherwise. (i) Normalising gives ∫₀¹ k(1 − x²)dx = k[x − x³/3]₀¹ = k(1 − 1/3) = 2k/3 = 1, so k = 3/2. (ii) The mean is E(X) = (3/2)∫₀¹ x(1 − x²)dx = (3/2)[x²/2 − x⁴/4]₀¹ = (3/2)(1/4) = 3/8 = 0.375. (iii) The second moment is E(X²) = (3/2)∫₀¹ x²(1 − x²)dx = (3/2)[x³/3 − x⁵/5]₀¹ = (3/2)(2/15) = 1/5, hence Var(X) = 1/5 − (3/8)² = 64/320 − 45/320 = 19/320 ≈ 0.0594.
questions.explanation: The normalisation condition fixes k, and integrating x f(x) and x^2 f(x) gives the mean and second moment required for the variance.

questions.q: 11 Probability density function of a random variable X is f(x) = {(1/2) sin x, for 0 <= x <= pi; 0, elsewhere}. Find the mean, mode and median of the distribution and also find the probability between 0 and pi/2. [L1][CO2] [10M]
questions.a: The density f(x) = (1/2)sin x on [0, π] is non-negative and integrates to (1/2)[−cos x]₀^π = 1, and it is symmetric about x = π/2. The mean is E(X) = (1/2)∫₀^π x sin x dx = (1/2)[−x cos x + sin x]₀^π = π/2. The density is largest where sin x = 1, namely at x = π/2, so the mode is π/2; by symmetry the median is also π/2. Finally, P(0 < X < π/2) = (1/2)∫₀^{π/2} sin x dx = (1/2)[−cos x]₀^{π/2} = 1/2.
steps: Verify normalisation: (1/2)[−cos x]₀^π = 1; density is symmetric about π/2
E(X) = (1/2)∫₀^π x sin x dx = (1/2)[−x cos x + sin x]₀^π = π/2
Mode: sin x is maximal at x = π/2; median by symmetry = π/2
questions.formula: Mean E(X)=∫x f(x)dx; mode = argmax f(x); median from F(m)=1/2
questions.explanation: The symmetric sine density is centred at pi/2 so the mean, mode and median coincide there, and the integral over half the support is exactly half the total probability.
